## What the model says

The memory measurement model (M3; [Oberauer & Lewandowsky, 2019](https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000159)),
implemented in the R package bmm, treats recall as a choice among response candidates, the options a
participant can give. Each candidate has an activation, how strongly it comes to mind, and candidates
with the same sources of activation form a category. In a simple-span task (bmm's version `ss`) there
are three categories: the item at the cued position (`corr`), the other list items (`other`), and
candidates that were not on the list (`npl`, not-presented lures). Their activations are

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_\text{corr} &= b + a + c \\
A_\text{other} &= b + a \\
A_\text{npl} &= b
\end{aligned}
$$

with background activation `b`, general activation `a` and context activation `c`. A choice rule turns
the activations into the probability $p_i$ that a response falls in category $i$. Each category is
weighted by its number of candidates $n_i$ ($n_\text{corr} = 1$, `n_other`, `n_npl`; `num_options` in
bmm), and $j$ runs over the three categories:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{simple:}&\quad p_i = \frac{n_i A_i}{\sum_j n_j A_j} \\[4pt]
\text{softmax:}&\quad p_i = \frac{n_i e^{A_i}}{\sum_j n_j e^{A_j}}
\end{aligned}
$$

`b` reaches every candidate. The simple rule gives the same probabilities when all activations are
multiplied by one constant, softmax when one constant is added to all of them, so one value has to be
fixed: bmm fixes `b` at 0.1 under the simple rule and at 0 under softmax. `a` reaches every item on
the studied list and lifts the cued item and the other list items above the lures. `c` comes from the
cue and reaches only the item at the cued position, so it separates the correct response from the
other list items.

## The task

One trial is cued recall from a candidate set. A list of letters is studied one at a time; then one
box is cued with a question mark, and the participant picks the letter that was in it from the
candidates on the screen. The candidates are the correct letter (blue), the other letters of the list
(orange) and letters that were not on the list (grey). Slots marked xxx are not in use on this trial.
Set size is the number of letters studied; `n_other` of the other list letters are offered at test,
so `n_other` is at most set size − 1. N is the number of candidates, 1 + `n_other` + `n_npl`.

## Explore

Each bar is the probability that the response on one trial falls in that category; the three add up
to 1. Raising `a` moves responses from the lures to the list, raising `c` from the other list items
to the correct one. Set size alone does not move the bars (see below). Reset restores the start.

The slider ranges come from bmm's default priors. The simple rule estimates log `a` with prior
normal(0, 1) and log `c` with normal(3, 1); softmax estimates `a` and `c` directly, both normal(3, 1).
Each slider spans the prior mean ± 3 SD: under the simple rule `a` runs from 0.05 to 20 and `c` from
1 to 403, under softmax both run from 0 to 6. The sliders start at the prior means, shown dashed.
Switching the rule restarts them there, because the same number means different things under the
two rules.

## Across task settings

The counts $n_i$ enter the probabilities $p_i$, and through them the likelihood (the probability the
model assigns to the observed responses). The model therefore predicts how recall changes with the
size of the response set without a new parameter: `a` and `c` stay as set; only the counts change.
Every added candidate adds to the denominator of the choice rule, so P(correct) falls as N grows.
Other list items have activation `b + a`, so for positive `a` they compete harder than lures, which
have only `b`.
<span id="m3-across-now"></span> These numbers follow the controls.

Set size is not in the likelihood of the simple-span version. It limits how many other list items can be
offered (at most set size − 1), and only that count enters. A longer list with the same response set
predicts the same proportions unless the bmm formula lets `a` or `c` differ between set sizes.

## In bmm

```{=html}
<div class="ex-widget">
  <pre class="ex-code" id="m3-code"></pre>
  <button type="button" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" id="m3-copy">Copy</button>
</div>
<script type="module" src="../js/pages/m3.js"></script>
```

The code updates with the controls. `m3()` defines the model (`version = "ss"` is the simple-span
version), `dm3()` returns the log probability of a set of response counts, and `bmf()` writes the
formula for `bmm()`, which estimates `a` and `c` from data; `my_data` stands for your own data, and
fitting runs Stan through brms. `b` is not passed: bmm adds it from the choice rule. See the [M3 article](https://venpopov.com/bmm/articles/bmm_m3.html) for the full model,
including the complex-span version and custom activation functions, and the reference pages for
[`m3()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/m3.html) and
[`dm3()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/m3dist.html).
